answer.rationale: Finance has mandated an 18% cut; the incumbent contract is expiring in 14 days without auto-renew, so the renewal price path is unlikely to yield an 18% reduction on its own. Memory c4 shows the incumbent can be moved on price, but typically by single-digit margins and on the timeline of a renewal cycle, not an 18% cut at this cadence. Memory c2 is the strongest directly-applicable lesson here: the prior switch to a low-cost primary vendor produced a sharp unit-cost cut last year with fast onboarding and accurate invoicing. Memory c6 (multi-year incumbency with the SAME vendor) is being deliberately NOT leveraged, because chasing volume-pricing locks deeper into a supplier whose unit cost is the problem, not the lever. The 94%-utilization, no-buffer line profile rules out 'add_second_source' as the single decision this cycle: parallel qualification costs throughput at exactly the wrong moment and does not directly address the mandated unit-cost cut. The expiring contract makes 'defer_decision' equivalent to losing the negotiation window. So: switch_primary_vendor (qualified low-cost vendor as new primary, incumbent off primary), scoped as a small guarded test on the highest-spend SKU first rather than a fleet-wide flip, with the existing incumbent retained as a backup second source (drawing on the risk-isolation lesson in c3) so delivery risk does not rise during ramp. I want c2 verified to confirm the onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy claim before I commit, because that is the load-bearing assumption. I want c4 verified because if the incumbent's recent quote is already materially below last year's, a partial switch becomes more attractive than a full switch, and c4 is the cleanest evidence I have about how much the incumbent will actually move.
